section.title: Local and absolute extrema
section.p: The sign chart for x^3-3x showed a graph that rises, then falls, then rises. At the point where rising changes to falling, the graph has a high point nearby. At the point where falling changes to rising, the graph has a low point nearby.

subsection.title: Local maximum and local minimum
subsection.p: A high point nearby is not necessarily the highest point everywhere. A mountain can have many peaks. A small peak is still a peak if the graph is lower on both sides nearby.

statement.p: A function f has a local maximum at c if
for all x sufficiently close to c.
A function f has a local minimum at c if
for all x sufficiently close to c.

subsection.p: The phrase sufficiently close means that we only compare f(c) with nearby values of the function. Local extrema are neighborhood ideas.
Now compare this with the global idea.

statement.p: A function f has an absolute maximum at c on a set D if
for every x\in D.
A function f has an absolute minimum at c on a set D if
for every x\in D.

subsection.p: Absolute extrema compare against the whole domain under discussion. Local extrema compare only nearby.

subsection.title: Fermat's theorem
subsection.p: At a smooth local maximum, the tangent line is horizontal. The graph rises into the point and falls away from it. The left-side slopes and right-side slopes force the tangent slope to be 0.
At a smooth local minimum, the same thing happens upside down.

There is no contradiction. Fermat's theorem applies to interior points, not endpoints. At an endpoint, the graph can be highest or lowest simply because the interval stops.

paragraphs.title: Corner warning
paragraphs.p: This function has a local minimum at x=0. But f'(0) does not exist. Again, Fermat's theorem is not contradicted. The theorem says that if the local extremum occurs at a differentiable interior point, then the derivative is 0.
Corners can have extrema without horizontal tangents.

subsection.title: The first derivative test
subsection.p: A critical number becomes more meaningful when we look at the sign of f' on both sides.

statement.p: Suppose c is a critical number of f, and f is continuous at c.

table.title: Classifications of critical points by the first derivative test

subsection.p: The reason is simple. If the function increases before c and decreases after c, then c is a high point nearby. If it decreases before c and increases after c, then c is a low point nearby.
This test depends on the first derivative sign rule, whose full proof comes from the Mean Value Theorem. The picture is already clear; the next theorem will make it secure.

subsection.title: Absolute extrema and the closed interval method
subsection.p: Local extrema are nearby comparisons. Absolute extrema are whole-domain comparisons. To find them, we need a guarantee that they exist.
The guarantee comes from continuity on a closed, bounded interval.

statement.p: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a,b], then f has an absolute maximum and an absolute minimum on [a,b].

subsection.p: This theorem is a deep fact about the real line. It rests on the idea that the real line has no gaps. For now, its meaning is more important than its proof:

blockquote.p: a continuous graph on a closed finite interval cannot escape its highest and lowest values.

subsection.p: The hypotheses matter.

paragraphs.title: Open interval warning
paragraphs.p: The function f(x)=x on (0,1) has no absolute maximum and no absolute minimum. Its values get close to 1, but never equal 1. They get close to 0, but never equal 0.

paragraphs.title: Unbounded interval warning
paragraphs.p: The function f(x)=x on [0,\infty) has an absolute minimum at 0, but no absolute maximum.

paragraphs.title: Continuity warning
paragraphs.p: on [0,1]. This function has no absolute maximum. The values approach 1, but the function never reaches 1. At the endpoint, it jumps down to 0.
The interval is closed and bounded, but the function is not continuous.

subsection.title: The closed interval method
subsection.p: Fermat's theorem tells us where an interior extremum can occur. The Extreme Value Theorem tells us that absolute extrema exist on a closed interval. Together they give a practical method.

statement.p: To find the absolute maximum and minimum of a continuous function f on [a,b]:

li.p: Find all critical numbers of f in (a,b).
Evaluate f at those critical numbers.
Compare the values. The largest is the absolute maximum value. The smallest is the absolute minimum value.

subsection.p: Endpoints are included because Fermat's theorem does not apply there. An endpoint can be the best or worst value simply because the graph stops.

subsection.title: Where this points
subsection.p: We have used the derivative to read the shape of a function:

Fermat's theorem was proved directly from the derivative definition. But the first derivative sign rule still needs its real proof.

The missing idea is surprisingly simple. If a car's average velocity over a trip is 50 miles per hour, then at some instant its speed should have been 50 miles per hour. If a smooth graph starts and ends at the same height, then somewhere in between it should have a horizontal tangent.
That idea is Rolle's Theorem, and just beyond it is the Mean Value Theorem.
